# Status report: jf2 allocator test in kestrel, 2026-11-20

## Short version

We tested jf2 (our fork of the jemalloc memory allocator) in kestrel (our key-value store) on a read-mostly workload. jf2 lowered p99 latency (the time within which 99% of requests finish) from 2140 us to 870 us, a 59% drop, with no measurable change in throughput or median latency. It also raised memory use by 5.7 GB (9.3%), which needs approval from the capacity team, and the write-heavy workload is not tested yet.

## Words used here

- **Build A**: commit 4f1c2aa of branch main with jemalloc 5.3 (the current allocator).
- **Build B**: the same commit with jf2 in place of jemalloc 5.3.
- **us**: microseconds.
- **kops/s**: thousand operations per second.
- **p50, p99, p99.9**: the time within which 50%, 99%, or 99.9% of requests finish.
- **Latency spike**: a short period when the slowest requests become much slower.
- **RSS**: resident set size, the physical memory the process holds.
- **Decay purge**: the step where jemalloc returns unused memory to the operating system.
- **ycsb-b, ycsb-a**: the read-mostly and the write-heavy workloads of YCSB (Yahoo Cloud Serving Benchmark).

## Test setup

- **Goal**: check whether jf2 removes the p99 latency spikes in kestrel.
- **Host**: bench-07 (2 x 32-core Xeon, 512 GB of memory, Linux kernel 6.8).
- **System load**: the load average before the runs was 0.4 (close to idle for a 64-core host).
- **Workload**: ycsb-b with 64 client threads.
- **Runs**: 5 runs per build, 10 minutes per run, in the order A, B, A, B, and so on.

## Results

```
p99 and p99.9 latency, median of 5 runs
(1 block = 250 us, shorter is better)

p99    A  █████████ 2140 us
       B  ███ 870 us                      (-59%)

p99.9  A  ███████████████████████████████████████ 9800 us
       B  ████████████ 3100 us            (-68%)
```

Only the slow requests changed: the p99 and p99.9 bars became shorter, and the table shows that throughput and p50 stayed the same.

| Metric | Build A (jemalloc 5.3) | Build B (jf2) | Change in median | Min-max ranges overlap? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Throughput (kops/s) | 412 (405 to 418) | 409 (401 to 415) | -3 (-0.7%) | Yes |
| p50 latency (us) | 118 (116 to 121) | 119 (117 to 121) | +1 (+0.8%) | Yes |
| p99 latency (us) | 2140 (1890 to 2610) | 870 (820 to 940) | -1270 (-59%) | No |
| p99.9 latency (us) | 9800 (7200 to 14100) | 3100 (2700 to 3900) | -6700 (-68%) | No |
| RSS at end of run (GB) | 61.2 | 66.9 | +5.7 (+9.3%) | No range recorded |

Each cell shows the median of 5 runs, with the minimum and maximum in parentheses.

- **p99 and p99.9 improved in every run.** The slowest build B run was faster than the fastest build A run on both metrics (p99: 940 us against 1890 us, p99.9: 3900 us against 7200 us).
- **Throughput and p50 show no measurable change.** The differences in the medians (3 kops/s and 1 us) are smaller than the range inside build A alone (13 kops/s and 5 us).
- **Memory use went up.** RSS at the end of the run was 5.7 GB higher with jf2.
- **Insufficient data on "fixed".** The notes give no target value for p99, so we cannot say whether 870 us meets the requirement.

## What the profile shows

- The spikes in build A occur at the same time as the jemalloc decay purge.
- In the spike windows, 31% of the samples from perf (the Linux profiler) were in `je_arena_decay` (the jemalloc function that does the purge).
- jf2 does the purge in a background thread.
- **Hypothesis**: moving the purge to the background thread is the reason for the lower p99. A perf profile of build B would confirm or reject this.

## Limits of this test

- **One run was replaced.** Run 3 of build B had a 40 s stall at minute 7. We traced the stall to the nightly logrotate job (a scheduled log clean-up task), not to the allocator. We reran it and used the rerun in the results.
- **Not tested:**
  - ycsb-a (the write-heavy workload)
  - more than 64 client threads
  - NUMA pinning (binding the process to the processors and memory of one socket)

## Open question

Is the RSS increase of 5.7 GB (9.3%) acceptable? We need an answer from the capacity team.

## Next steps

1. Run ycsb-a tomorrow.
2. Ask the capacity team about the RSS increase.
3. If the capacity team approves, enable jf2 in staging (the pre-production environment), controlled by a configuration flag.

---

**Added beyond your notes; check before sending:**

- The percent changes for throughput, p50, p99, and p99.9 are computed from your medians.
- The "ranges overlap" column and the two bullets built on it are my reading of your min-max values.
- The "Insufficient data" bullet about a missing p99 target is my addition.
- I labeled the background-thread explanation a hypothesis, since your notes have a perf profile for build A only.
- The one-line descriptions of ycsb-b and ycsb-a use the standard YCSB definitions. Correct them if your workload files differ.
